input:
Feedback control is used throughout the process industries to keep important variables at the values required, and a temperature loop on a process vessel illustrates the principles involved. The loop consists of several distinct elements, and its operation can be understood by following the signal from one element to the next.

The first element is the sensor, whose task is to measure the temperature of the vessel contents and convert the measurement into a signal the other elements can use. Thermocouples and resistance thermometers are commonly employed for this purpose, and what the loop requires of the instrument is an accurate and responsive measurement of the temperature as it stands.

The controller receives the signal from the sensor and compares the measured temperature with the desired value, establishing the difference between them, which is known as the error. On the basis of the error, the controller produces an output calling for the heating or cooling applied to the vessel to be increased or decreased, as circumstances require.

The final element carries out the adjustment to the process, and in a temperature loop it is normally a control valve in the line supplying the heating medium or the line supplying the cooling medium. As the valve responds to the controller output, the flow of the medium changes, and the temperature of the contents changes in consequence.

Of particular importance is the sign of the feedback, which in a correctly arranged loop is negative. If the temperature rises above the desired value, the loop responds in the direction that brings it down again, and if it falls below, the response raises it once more, so that every departure provokes a reaction that works against it.
target:
A temperature loop holds the temperature in a process vessel at the value the process requires, acting on the heating or cooling supply as the temperature moves. The loop has four parts: the sensor, the controller, the final element, and the sign of the feedback.

The sensor measures the temperature of the vessel contents and turns the measurement into a signal. A thermocouple or a resistance thermometer can serve; what the loop asks of the sensor is a faithful and prompt report of the temperature as it now stands.

The controller receives the sensor signal and compares the measured temperature with the set value, and the difference between them is the error. From the error the controller forms an output that calls for heating or cooling to be raised or lowered, in the direction the error requires and by an amount that grows with the error.

The final element acts on the process. In a temperature loop the final element is a control valve on the line that feeds the heating medium to the vessel, or on the line that feeds the cooling medium, and the valve changes the flow of that medium as the controller output changes. The temperature follows the flow.

The sign of the feedback is negative. A temperature above the set value calls out action that brings the temperature down, and a temperature below the set value calls out action that brings it up: the response works against the deviation, and the loop returns the temperature to the set value.
